As a foundation for work on computability theory and Turing machines, I'd like to discuss some general definitions for this area.

In particular, I think there should be some typeclass capturing the idea of a computation based on an "atomic" step operation of some configuration state, a property that (to the best of my knowledge) all Turing machine-type computation models share (and also some other forms of computation that are not turing machines).

Specifically, in my projects I've been working with these so far:

/-- Bundle of a type `σ` with a step function `σ → Option σ`. -/
class TransitionModel (τ : Type*) where
  σ (a : τ) : Type
  step {a : τ} : σ a → Option (σ a)

/-- An abstract version of a computer with input alphabet `Γ₀` and output alphabet `Γ₁`. -/
class TransitionComputer (τ : Type*) (Γ₀ Γ₁ : Type) extends TransitionModel τ where
  init {a : τ} : List Γ₀ → σ a
  output {a : τ} : σ a → List Γ₁

We can think of the type τ as a model computation. For example, τ could be the type of all single-tape turing machines with a fixed alphabet (SingleTapeTM Symbol in current cslib). σ a then represents Turing.SingleTapeTM.Cfg, the configuration of such a machine (i.e. state of program + current tape).
So you would naturally have SingleTapeTM Symbol get the instance: TransitionComputer (SingleTapeTM Symbol) Symbol Symbol := sorry.
Similarly, this would also work if τ is the type of multi-tape turing machines (with fixed input/output alphabet), or turing machines with access to some (fixed) oracle, etc.

We can then define all of the common notions of computable (within a time function), reductions, transformations, complexity classes like P / NP with respect to such a model. Then you can also precisely write down what it means for two such models of computation to be equivalent (up to some factor, typically polynomial), and from that reduce that the definition of P (NP, ...) is agnostic to which computation model you use (as long as they are equivalent up to poly-time).

Further down the line, I could also think of using τ as representing terms in λ-calculus, and steps being term reductions, or similar applications, so that we can also fit other forms of "computation" in this model, prove equivalence and thus transfer results about existence of computability between various different kinds of computation models.

Right now, I'd be asking for feedback regarding the design choices above. In particular, these are the ones that I used for my previous student project (which was based on mathlib still, see here: https://git.abstractnonsen.se/max/mathlib4), where in particular I used them to define P / NP and prove that for the two turing models TM0 and TM1 that were present in mathlib, these yield the same definition. I have found it useful to work with them, but I'm curious about thoughts from others.

I am not sure about the naming in particular. I don't think it should involve "Turing", because it's not really about Turing machines specifically and we might have other applications in the future. Open to suggestions.

I have outlined some first definitions using this design pattern and put up a draft PR on github for this, see https://github.com/leanprover/cslib/pull/550.

Note also the related topic https://leanprover.zulipchat.com/#narrow/channel/513188-CSLib/topic/Outputs.20of.20Turing.20machines/with/593181144: My current design choice is to have this function

output {a : τ} : σ a → List Γ₁

which right now is not what we do for single tape turing machines.
If we were to stick with the current implementation, we should replace this output function by a "many-to-at-most-one" relation, presumably σ a → Option (List Γ₁) (since output should clearly be unique if it exists).

I like the definitions a lot but we should maybe use names that are a bit more suggestive. I agree that “Turing” should not be part of it, but we could use the term “Machine” or “TransitionSystem”. About the second item: if something computes an output from an input it is sometimes called “transducer”, although I don’t know how general the term ist. Sometimes it is used to distinguish from “acceptor” which can only give a boolean output.
Also for the fields, I would use cfg, config or something similar instead of sigma (especially confusing since sigma is sometimes used for the step function, so if we stay with a greek letter then maybe gamma). About the alphabets: is (sorry, cannot type Unicode here) \Gamma_in / \Gamma_out too complicated?

Thanks for the suggestions! I think Transducer is a good term that captures what this is meant to be. Regarding the fields: Yeah, probably fair to have a more meaningful name there. I did introduce the notation σ[tm] to mean the application (σ tm), because you deal with the type a lot and it is cumbersome to put it into parantheses all the time. Maybe we should also come up with a better notation there (or accept to use parantheses and always open the namespace to shorten).
Γ_in and Γ_out seeem okay to me (though annoying to write all the time maybe), not sure what typical naming conventions are used in cslib.
Note that we already have P and NP in Algolean
Well, I want to have it in CSLib, too, hence this discussion
Of course. This is only to offer a design for comparison

Yes, I saw σ[tm] in the PR, and I think the following comment applies to σ[tm] as well as Γ_in and Γ_out: The Basic.lean file is probably read much more than it is written. Since Γ_in and Γ_out are positional parameters, I think users of the file probably won't write it much. I'm not so sure about σ[tm], though. I found it a bit confusing, and I think parentheses are probably a small burden to pay here. Not to open that can of worms, but I just want to mention it: I know mathlib (and probably also cslib) uses \Gamma for alphabets, but I am more used to \Sigma. Not sure if there is some kind of consensus about that... Again, this is not important.

I wanted to comment on the PR itself, but github seems too have difficulties, so let me write it here: In my work, I found myself referring to the function fun cfg t => (flip bind step)^[t] (some cfg) a lot. Maybe this should merit a name like configSequence / configs? I also found it easier to work with than the "reachable in steps" relation (especially since a relation per so is not necessarily "linear") and Iterate.lean in mathlib provides nice lemmas to use for induction or composition.

Shreyas Srinivas said:

Note that we already have P and NP in Algolean

Whether it is intended or not, when you frequently come to the CSLib channel and say just "X is already in Algolean", it is not conducive to a productive conversation. If you are discussing upstreaming something or making a particular technical comparison that is fine, but otherwise a message like the above seems off-topic.

Upstreaming it would be desirable . That is why I mentioned it. That is why the design comparison makes sense. Conversely we would adopt or adapt to the final CSLib version that comes out of the comparison if the definition is useful and different from ours.

This looks promising, but I've always wondered: why not just use/extend F(LTS) so to inherit notions of multistep, reachability, behavioural equivalences, etc.? (Outside of convenience for dealing with the identification of termination thanks to Option, which we might be able to deal with in a couple of ways.)

Is there something we need to generalise? Or is it fundamentally unfeasible to wrap it into an 'expected' TM API?

Especially if we're looking at a transducer, that can be an LTS with a label type that is a pair (input and output), or an LTS where states are configurations (state with output string so far), etc. We can then give it a relational interface as expected.

(This also makes me wonder a bit if LTS should provide a class to access its API.)

Good question @Fabrizio Montesi . I haven't really thought in that direction so far, but to me it feels strange to use the same interface: What is the Label type of an LTS meant to represent in the case of a turing machine?

Fabrizio Montesi said:

Especially if we're looking at a transducer, that can be an LTS with a label type that is a pair (input and output), or an LTS where states are configurations (state with output string so far), etc. We can then give it a relational interface as expected.

I didn't understand what you mean here. If the label type is a pair (input / output), then what is the state transition function meant to represent (assuming that the state type of the LTS corresponds to the current configuration of the TM)?

My conceptual understanding is that an LTS represents a "nondeterministic" transition system, where each transition is indicated by which label you choose. With turing machines (at least deterministic ones), this is not the case, we really only have a transition function State → State, together with some abstraction of input / output from/to lists of symbols.
And if we were to choose a unit type as labels, then I don't see the point in using the LTS API anymore.

I'd be happy for some more explanation / detail on how you would model a Turing machine (say, singe-tape with input/output on that tape for now) as an LTS, i.e. what the State and Label types would correspond to.

chris477 said:

I wanted to comment on the PR itself, but github seems too have difficulties, so let me write it here: In my work, I found myself referring to the function fun cfg t => (flip bind step)^[t] (some cfg) a lot. Maybe this should merit a name like configSequence / configs? I also found it easier to work with than the "reachable in steps" relation (especially since a relation per so is not necessarily "linear") and Iterate.lean in mathlib provides nice lemmas to use for induction or composition.

I agree that this is an important function, and it is more convenient than the RelatesWithinSteps framework, just because we are dealing with the special case of a function and thus have a more 'linear' sequence. It's not part of the current PR, but I'll definitely include things in that direction (and some theorems on how that sequence tells us about output / runtime etc) in the future.

Right. Some of the following might be original ideas (though I can see some similarities with Reactive Turing Machines, minus the communication channels), and I might be overengineering. However, I find it interesting to discuss especially because we're talking about finding generalisations, and maybe we want multiple versions that can be converted into one another (perhaps through instances) depending on what's more convenient. We had similar discussions for automata. Here goes:

Maximilian Keßler said:

Good question Fabrizio Montesi . I haven't really thought in that direction so far, but to me it feels strange to use the same interface: What is the Label type of an LTS meant to represent in the case of a turing machine?

Depends on what you're interested in defining as the 'interesting observable behaviour' of the machine. A choice can be to have transition labels that define the input symbol, the output symbol, and the movement of the head. Another could be to have only the input symbol.
For the former, you can decide further if the LTS has the tape state in each state or not (if not, then you'd obtain a 'true' TM by plumbing the LTS with a tape).

FLTS would cover deterministic TMs and LTS (potentially) nondeterministic TMs.

For transducers (which are connected), I've made a quick attempt at formulating a simple transducer (without epsilon symbols) here:
https://github.com/leanprover/cslib/compare/main...transducer

Here, I'd be surprised if the 'pair of input and output symbol' trick is new.
(I made a thread for the #CSLib > Transducers to avoid derailing this discussion with that specific case too much.)

Okay, thanks for the clarification.
While I think that the Transducer typeclass that you lined out might be useful (it's very analogue to what an Acceptor is, which we already have in CSLib), it doesn't capture everything that we would like to care about when we talk about Turing machine executions, since the typeclass gives us no access to the number of execution steps needed to perform the translation of strings.

So to me the direction in which you are going (about using LTS to model turing machines) does not seem to be the right fit.

However, I agree that what we call a transducer probably shouldn't inherently talk about runtime as well, i.e. we should choose a different name for the definition I suggested:

/-- An abstract version of a computer with input alphabet `Γ₀` and output alphabet `Γ₁`. -/
class TransitionComputer (τ : Type*) (Γ₀ Γ₁ : Type) extends TransitionModel τ where
  init {a : τ} : List Γ₀ → σ a
  output {a : τ} : σ a → List Γ₁

because it isn't quite a transducer. However, there is a canonical instance synthesis here:

instance [TransitionComputer τ Γ₀ Γ₁] : Transducer τ  Γ₀ Γ₁ where
   Translates a xs ys = TransitionComputer.Outputs a xs ys

(where TransitionComputer.Outputs is the Output structure which I defined in my PR already)
which essentially stems from "forgetting" about execution steps and abstracting away the execution states.

So I would suggest to have both typeclasses in CSLib, whereas I would (mostly) be working with what I called TransitionComputer here.

Maximilian Keßler said:

Note also the related topic https://leanprover.zulipchat.com/#narrow/channel/513188-CSLib/topic/Outputs.20of.20Turing.20machines/with/593181144: My current design choice is to have this function

output {a : τ} : σ a → List Γ₁

which right now is not what we do for single tape turing machines.
If we were to stick with the current implementation, we should replace this output function by a "many-to-at-most-one" relation, presumably σ a → Option (List Γ₁) (since output should clearly be unique if it exists).

I think I actually take this back and would prefer to have

output {a : τ} : σ a → Option (List Γ₁)

instead, just because it is slightly more flexible / general when it comes to defining instances of this class, and definitions wouldn't really change anyways.

This will also have the advantage that we can theoretically define both types of "output" on turing machine (tape is output exactly vs. we take output to the right of the head in the halt state), giving us two instances, for which we can then prove equivalence.

Generally, I would like for the design choices made here to be flexible enough that we can have "plenty" variants of definitions of Turing machines (or other step-based computation models), a general set of definitions for them + equivalence proofs. Then whenever you want to work with Turing machines, you can pick the specific model suitable for your application and use the general equivalence theorem to reason that your specific choice did not matter.

Maximilian Keßler said:

Okay, thanks for the clarification.
While I think that the Transducer typeclass that you lined out might be useful (it's very analogue to what an Acceptor is, which we already have in CSLib), it doesn't capture everything that we would like to care about when we talk about Turing machine executions, since the typeclass gives us no access to the number of execution steps needed to perform the translation of strings.

So to me the direction in which you are going (about using LTS to model turing machines) does not seem to be the right fit.

Transducer and DA.FinTransducer are an example of how to do a Transducer class and implement it with an LTS.

If you wanna know how much time, space, communications, or other things a machine used for a concrete execution, wouldn't LTS.Execution be appropriate? (If we end up deciding we don't want labels, we can define the same concept for Relation.)

(As I hinted at, I picked Transducer to have a simpler example.)

To be clear, I'm not saying we don't need machine classes. I'm just trying to see if we can avoid redefining multistep transitions, reachability, termination, etc., by trying to reuse Relation or LTS (at least for the concrete structure representing a TM). Discussing the machine classes is still valid. These should be as abstract as possible.
It could also be that we wanna have a class that (perhaps specific uses of) LTS and Relation are instances of.. for example to define the number of steps needed, etc.

I tend to agree with @Fabrizio Montesi here. In my recent work on formalizing a famous result in distributed computing:
#CSLib > Impossibility of distributed consensus
I could easily use LTS to model distributed systems and their finite and infinite executions and leverage many results we have already proved for LTS to prove results about distributed systems. An LTS is a very general notion, as the types of its "states" and "labels" are completely uninterpreted and can be instantiated to anything you like.

I took a more thorough look at what concepts / theorems etc we have about LTS in CSLib right now. Here is some of the thoughts that I have regarding using LTS to model turing machine (or generally computation)-related concepts using an LTS.

Let us say that we want to model a turing machine using some LTS. The most obvious way to do that (at least for me), would be to use State = configurations of the tm while execution, Label = Unit and tr relates two configurations if they differ by a single instruction execution of the tm. While this works and allows us to define things like multi-step transition, reachability etc, it is, in some sense, cumbersome: We are now dealing with an LTS that has many more properties, since it is linear (if you think about the graph structure), and the label type is reduntant. This also means that many things like LTS.Execution are cumbersome to work with, since they are much more general than needed for this use-case. I think this justifies to "repeat" (or maybe specialize) such definitions for (deterministic) computation processes and not work with the generic LTS definitions.

Fabrizio Montesi said:

If you wanna know how much time, space, communications, or other things a machine used for a concrete execution, wouldn't LTS.Execution be appropriate? (If we end up deciding we don't want labels, we can define the same concept for Relation.)

So yes, intuitively, I would like that, and I'd be happy to define such things for relations. It might even be useful to define it for relations that are of the form r a b := f a = b for a function f, which is the case for turing machines, because this simplifies things further (and this is essentially what my current outlined PR is doing).

Regarding the transducer example: I can see how an LTS can be used to define a transducer, but I don't think we can view a turing machine as such a transducer: If we use the (input output pair) labeling system (as in @Fabrizio Montesi 's outlined PR), then (at least as I see it), we lose track of the actual execution time of the TM.

Fabrizio Montesi said:

It could also be that we wanna have a class that (perhaps specific uses of) LTS and Relation are instances of.. for example to define the number of steps needed, etc.

Yes, I could imagine that. On the other hand, is this not essentially what RelatesInSteps is doing? We could introduce one more typeclass that just bundles the relation which semantically is "one execution step", and then define attributes about running times in terms of this class, but I think it would mostly be a wrapper around RelatesInSteps, and I'm unsure how much this will be needed. But it would fit, and a computation model (how I outlined such classes) could also be an instance of this class.

Another thing that I want to mention is that to establish equivalences up to poly-time factors, it has been useful to work with what is essentially a weaker version of bisimilarity, which allows for a transition in the first LTS to be modelled by a (bounded) amount of transitions in the second LTS before states need to be related again.
See https://git.abstractnonsen.se/max/mathlib4/src/commit/0f4c50edbe7ac8b5f92fee9f514b4385446c4bd6/Mathlib/Computability/TuringBase.lean#L95 for such a definiton, and https://git.abstractnonsen.se/max/mathlib4/src/commit/0f4c50edbe7ac8b5f92fee9f514b4385446c4bd6/Mathlib/Computability/TuringBase.lean#L116, https://git.abstractnonsen.se/max/mathlib4/src/commit/0f4c50edbe7ac8b5f92fee9f514b4385446c4bd6/Mathlib/Computability/TuringBase.lean#L156 for the corresponding results that allow one to deduce that computations yield the same results in poly-time factors from such a relation.

I imagine that such things could be generalized and then ported to the machine-world (as result specializations), and this is a direction I'd be happy to work towards.

Generally, to me it currently seems that LTS's have some general notions that we can re-use for turing machines as well as some results (like the above), but at the same time, it will be nice to specialize a lot of them because we don't need their full generality.
That's also why I would like to avoid defining things in terms of an LTS, because then definitions might always be a littlebit annoying to work with, whereas in proof contexts, we might make good use of LTS's.

I also updated my PR https://github.com/leanprover/cslib/pull/550 and would in principle be happy for it to be considered for merging / continue discussing whether we want to change what definitions to work with
@Sorrachai Yingchareonthawornchai @Fabrizio Montesi

We cannot do TMs with my transducer, it was just an example of how to do an 'interesting' label type. Again, for a TM, I'd probably either use something like 'input symbol, output symbol, movement' (and then bundle it with a tape) or 'input symbol' (here the tape would be already in the structure).

But I realise this discussion might be a bit abstract, while you're doing the great thing of showing us concrete code, so I'm gonna try to write something more precise down.. :-)

It might still be rough around the edges, but this is more or less what I meant, exemplified for nondeterministic turing machines: https://github.com/leanprover/cslib/compare/main...fmontesi/tm-lts

It shows (unless I got a definition wrong) that an NTM is nothing else than a specific nondeterministic automaton equipped with a tape. I then instantiate Acceptor to obtain the language of an NTM as we normally do for the other automata.

For TMs, one can do something similar with a deterministic automaton. There are many flavours of (N)TMs, here I've just chosen the one that fit best.

One could also instantiate the Transducer class I wrote in the other branch for transducers (a TM is a translator as well as an acceptor).

This still requires some work though, to make proving theorems about it a bit more ergonomic.

Btw, an alternative is to just say that an NTM extends an NA.FinAcc with a tape.

Even for deterministic TM, I think LTS is a more appropriate framework than FLTS. The PR cslib#550 uses a partial transition function to model the transition relation of a deterministic TM. But a partial transition function is equivalent to a deterministic LTS:
https://api.cslib.io/docs/Cslib/Foundations/Semantics/LTS/Basic.html#Cslib.LTS.Deterministic
where the label type can be set to Unit if we don't care about transition labels. Currently not many properties about deterministic LTS have been proved, but they can be easily added.

Worked a bit more on this, and polished https://github.com/leanprover/cslib/compare/main...fmontesi/tm-lts

A mini recap and my two cents:

Following textbook presentations, the signature of an NTM (which, notably, does not include configurations but just what I'd call the 'controller') matches quite well that of an NA equipped with a set of halting states. Here using LTS looks natural. So we obtain:

/-- A (single-tape) Nondeterministic Turing Machine (NTM) is a nondeterministic automaton equipped
with a set of accepting halting states. -/
structure SingleTapeNTM (State Symbol : Type*)
    extends NA State (SingleTapeNTM.TrLabel State Symbol) where
  /-- The set of accepting states. -/
  accept : Set State
  /-- Proof that all accepting states are halting states. -/
  accept_halting (hmem : s ∈ accept) : ¬∃ μ s', Tr s μ s'

At this point we can easily define the expected operational semantics for configurations that an NTM yields, either in terms of an LTS with Unit labels or a reduction relation:

-- As an LTS
@[scoped grind =]
def SingleTapeNTM.cfgLts {Symbol} (m : SingleTapeNTM State Symbol) : LTS (Cfg State Symbol) Unit where
  Tr c _ c' :=
    ∃ μ, m.Tr c.state μ c'.state ∧ -- The controller can perform the move
      μ.read = c.tape.head ∧ -- The tape has the expected symbol to be read
      c'.tape = (c.tape.write μ.write).optionMove μ.move -- Write effect on the tape

-- As a reduction relation
@[scoped grind =]
def SingleTapeNTM.Red {Symbol} (m : SingleTapeNTM State Symbol)
    (c c' : Cfg State Symbol) : Prop :=
  ∃ μ, m.Tr c.state μ c'.state ∧ -- The controller can perform the move
    μ.read = c.tape.head ∧ -- The tape has the expected symbol to be read
    c'.tape = (c.tape.write μ.write).optionMove μ.move -- Write effect on the tape

The former (LTS) automatically gives us all derived definitions, like multistep reductions, executions, omega-executions, etc. The latter (Red) doesn't, we have to do it manually because we've recently reverted ReductionSystem into using plain-old relations. ReductionSystem was how we were modelling transition systems without labels. So I have the feeling that if we still had ReductionSystem, it'd have provided at least some of what @Maximilian Keßler is trying to do here. @Maximilian Keßler, do you agree? The old ReductionSystem would have basically allowed you to define a Red relation like above, and then you'd give multistep execution and all related classes for free (diamond, some closure properties, etc.).

@Chris Henson, we're looking at essentially the same abstraction that people use for reduction semantics (e.g., as in lambda calculus). Opinions?

I think @Maximilian Keßler does not ignore the labels entirely, because he wants to count the number of steps so that he can talk about time complexity (see cslib#550). So LTS's with a singleton label type, not reduction systems, are what he needs. Note that if Label is a singleton type, elements of List Label are completely determined by their lengths.

Thanks for getting back to this @Fabrizio Montesi .
First toanswer your specific question:
I don't know the details of what your ReductionSystem used to do, but yes, in principle the abstract view on turing machines that I wanted to take is "Transition system without labels", so this seems like the thing I would want to work with.

Thanks for your example of the NTM definition, I understand now what you mean by using an LTS with a non-unit label type to model turing machines.
If I see this correctly, what you outlined is essentially "the definition" of a single-tape non-deterministic turing machine, i.e. specification of the 'controller' and the 'configuration' + execution semantics, in analogue on how we already have a definition of single-tape deterministic turing machines in Machines/SingleTapeTuring/Basic.lean, and I can see how it might be useful to re-use the LTS semantics here (and the ReductionSystem semantics, in case we still were to have them).

However, I think that this is actually a different (though related) topic to the one I had in mind when creating this thread and outlining my PR:
I want to develop typeclasses with the following properties

  • SingleTapeTM, MultiTapeTM, etc can be made instances of this typeclass, giving meaning to "how" these a priori unrelated models of computation can be embedded into the same framework
  • We can define input / output / execution time / space / ... dependent on this typeclass and then inherit the specific definitions for individual models of computation via the provided instances
  • Future work: We can also view things like λ-calculus as instances, by defining appropriate versions of execution time / space / etc.
    Regarding the "framework" that I wanted to work with, I wanted to outline this in the first post of this thread.
    The TransitionModel definition I wrote down there is essentially a (deterministic) version of the Red relation you defined for SingleTapeNTM - or in the case of SingleTapeTM it corresponds to SingleTapeTM.step : tm.Cfg → tm.Cfg.
    The theory of only TransitionModel thus seems to be the theory of (deterministic) reduction systems = labelled (deterministic) transition systems with unit label type.
    However, the important thing for me was to combine this with init and output functions in the TransitionComputer class: This means that we can deduce[Transducer t Symbol Symbol] or [Acceptor t Symbol] from [TransitionComputer t Symbol Symbol], but also have more fine-grained access to execution semantics (like number of execution steps) about how the transducer operates while still being model-agnostic on the specific version of TMs that we are working with.
    In particular, your definition
@[simp, scoped grind =]
instance {Symbol} : Acceptor (SingleTapeNTM State Symbol) Symbol where
  Accepts (m : SingleTapeNTM State Symbol) (xs : List Symbol) :=
    ∃ s ∈ m.start, ∃ c', m.MRed {state := s, tape := Turing.BiTape.mk₁ xs} c'

combines two things: It talks about the execution of an NTM (via m.MRed), but also what it means to "start" with xs : List Symbol (namely {state := s, tape := Turing.BiTape.mk₁ xs}).
My approach / goal with the typeclasses outlined was to separate these two, and use this init xs := {state := s, tape := Turing.BiTape.mk₁ xs} function as part of the exposed typeclasse, which allows us to define such an Acceptor instance for other kinds of turing machines with a single definition.

So I feel like we are trying to answer different questions here (and for some time in this thread, tried to answer different ones):

  • Do we want to use an LTS to model turing machines (future variants of them, but also potentially re-desingn the existing SingleTapeTM we have)?
  • Do we want to use an LTS to model "computation models"?
  • Do we want to bundle the LTS (or reduction system) on a "configuration type" with input / output semantics
    For the first question, I think the answer is "yes" (as you and others have pointed out), for the second question I still think it is "no", because model-agnostically, we would work with a unit-label type, and therefore should rather work with a ReductionSystem.
    The third question is what I'm trying to answer with the TransitionComputer from my initial post here and which I proposed.

I also feel like I might be repeating myself at this point and my post has become very lengthy.
In case you (and / or others) would be willing to do that, I would also be open to have a (short) call about some of these designs, since I think this might be helpful / simplify some of the conversation.

So SingleTapeNTM.red m : Rel (Cfg State Symbol) is just a relation and totally fine to work with, and the equivalent of fun a b => step a = some b from my initial post.
I would prefer working with such a relatio

Potentially relevant question: Would more code examples be helpful to further judge what I'm trying to do here?

About the list of questions that @Maximilian Keßler asked above: I personally believe that the following two notions should be decoupled:
(1) the computational models (Turing machines, lambda calculus, distributed algorithms, ...);
(2) the (labeled or unlabeled) state transition systems that those models generate.
The reason for this decoupling is simple: we don't want to re-define and re-prove common notions in (2) (like finite or infinite executions with or without intermediate states, finite and infinite concatenation of executions, ...) again and again for different models of computation. They should be done once and for all in the most general form and specialized to specific cases.

The one thing I do want to avoid is that for defining these different types that you are forced to use some particular unifying framework. There are differences between these "models" (see this post about lambda calculus and Turing machines for instance) that I want to make sure we don't lose, along with making individual definitions work well for that specialization.

Concretely the reason I removed ReductionSystem (in CSLib#320) is that it's a pain to keep things in duplicate for bundled and unbundled relations, the latter which we inherit from core and Mathlib. I'm not opposed to additional abstractions, but I don't think we're going to see something that everyone agrees on as "the" model of computation.

Note that I was not saying we should have a single model of computation. But I was saying we shouldn't have state transition systems and associated notions and results being formalized again and again in different models of computation.

That is interesting to note, and in fact something I hadn't thought about so far, so let me outline a bit more what I wanted to get at.

Let us assume for now that we have agreed on some established theory of transition systems (be it using ReductionSystem, RelatesInSteps or LTR, etc). In my inital post I introduced TransitionModel for this, and I agree we might not need this after all because it is re-doing existing things.

My motivation for introducing the outlined typeclasses is to be able to state computation classes, in particular P, NP and NPComplete.

Classical definitions of these rely on languages over (finite) alphabets and thus talk about how words over this alphabet relate to the state transition systems described by our computation model. To define P and NP, we need to convert an "input" into a "first state" before we can run a transition system to get a yes/no output. However, to define NP-completeness, we also need to talk about computability of functions between (potentially different) alphabets, since we need to define what a "polynomial transformation" is.

Thus, the TransitionComputer class that I outlined was a try to define the "minimial" interface that we need to define what P and NP are (or actually, you need a family of TransitionComputer for any two (finite) alphabet types to define them), and we necessarily need to talk about more than just transition systems for this task.

In the end what I would like to be able is to have definitions like

def P (t : Type*) [SomeClass t] : Set Language := sorry
def NP (t : Type*) [SomeClass t] : Set Language := sorry
def NPComplete (t : Type*) [SomeClass t] : SetLanguage := sorry

and then be able to proof things like

lemma P_eq (t t' : Type*) [SomeClass t] [SomeClass t'] (h : PolyEquivalent t t') : P t = P t' := sorry
lemma NPC_eq (t t' : Type*) [SomeClass t] [SomeClass t'] (h : PolyEquivalent t t') : NPComplete t = NPComplete t' := sorry
example : P SingleTapeTM = P MultiTapeTM := by
    apply P_eq
    apply some_equivalence_theorem
    ...
example : P SingleTapeTM = P LambdaCalculus := sorry

(this is a bit pseudocode, since we probably need a thing which syntactically is not the existing SingleTapeTM).
Here, [SomeClass t] would model that from t we can get types t Γ₀ Γ₁ that satisfy [TransitionComputer (t Γ₀ Γ₁) Γ₀ Γ₁] and which we then can use to define P and friends.

For all of this, as far as I'm aware, your distinction between encoding functions in λ-calculus and turing machines does not matter, since (as you mentioned) the church-turing hypothesis "holds" also for functions between languages over finite alphabets.

If we're talking about higher-order functions (like in the post you referenced), then we probably need other mechanism to state those definitions anyway, and (at least for now) this is not what I intend to be working on.

Not wanting to make this topic even more complicated, but I have been working on a computation model that is not step-based (i.e. not a transition system) and whose internal data structure is also not a string. It can be found here - I was able to define a simulation of Single-Tape-TM and prove it semantically correct in a few days, so I think it has merit - of course there are still several things missing like the other direction ;).

But this comment is not about that, it's more about the fact that we should not restrict ourselves to transition based systems and maybe also not to string-based encodings because there are convenient and useful machine models that do not have these properties. Of course it also makes a lot of sense to create a common structure for all computations that are step-based, but I think we should go further than that for defining computation models and their complexities.

I created a PR about an abstract machine model and associated type encodings. It is similar to Blum's complexity measures in that it only defines a function that returns the time and space complexity of a computation on a certain input.

I will not repeat all the details from the PR here, but just want to say that it has an example where lambda calculus is shown to be a machine model in that sense, and it makes the point that it's very convenient that you don't have to encode lambda terms into strings and decode them again if you don't require the computation to be based on strings. Because of that, encodings of data types should be machine-model specific (although they should be "size-compatible" in a certain sense).

Furthermore, if we go that route, I think we can prove certain theorems like the time hierarchy theorem without having to explicitly spell out the Turing machines involved. We can do that in a way that we require certain properties of a machine model (there is a universal machine, the snm-theorem holds, boolean negation is computable in constant space and linear time, function composition is computable in constant additional time and constant additional space, constructing a pair and destructuring a pair is computable in certain time and space, etc) and prove the theorem just based on these properties. But then the properties are not axioms because we can prove them for certain machine models and get complexity results like that for all machine models that fulfill these properties (i.e. all sane machine models).

And finally: If this plan works out, we can also swap out the machine model "in the middle of a proof" because we have a theorem that asserts their equivalence.
